posts.title: Agent Memory: Treating the Context Window Like RAM, Not Storage
posts.subtitle: MemGPT's OS-inspired trick lets an agent hold a lifetime of conversation inside a context window built for a few thousand tokens.
posts.summary: An LLM agent's context window is fast but tiny and stateless between calls. MemGPT's virtual context management borrows the classic OS trick of treating scarce fast memory as a cache over larger, slower storage — letting an agent self-manage what's in its context window via ordinary function calls, and giving it memory that survives well past any single conversation.

slides.title: Your Agent Forgets Everything the Moment It Overflows
slides.body: A context window feels like the model's whole mind, but it's really a fixed-size buffer. Once a conversation or task outgrows it, something has to be dropped — unless the agent manages its own memory the way an operating system manages RAM.

slides.title: Fixed Context, Unbounded Conversations
bullets: A context window (say 128K-500K tokens) is fast and directly attended-over, but it's finite — and every message, tool call, and tool result eats into it
Naive truncation (drop the oldest messages) silently loses information the agent may need later, with no signal that anything was lost
Naive summarization burns extra LLM calls and compresses away exactly the low-level details (a specific number, a exact file path) that later steps often need
Neither approach gives the agent persistent memory across separate sessions — each new conversation starts from zero regardless of history

slides.title: Virtual Context Management: Borrow the OS's Memory Hierarchy
slides.body: MemGPT (Packer et al., 'Towards LLMs as Operating Systems') reframes the context window as RAM: scarce, fast, and directly usable — with external stores playing the role of disk.
bullets: Main context (in the prompt) = RAM: what the model can directly attend over right now
Recall storage = a complete, queryable log of the full conversation history, outside the active context
Archival storage = a searchable long-term database for arbitrary facts, notes, and documents the agent chooses to save
The agent moves data between these tiers itself, using ordinary function calls — no special infrastructure beyond tool use

slides.title: Self-Editing Memory via Interrupts
slides.body: When main context nears its limit, the system triggers a kind of interrupt: the model is prompted to decide what to evict to recall storage and, if relevant, what to page in from archival storage — before continuing the task.
bullets: Eviction and retrieval are function calls the model itself invokes (e.g. save_to_archival, search_archival) — the model is an active participant in managing its own memory, not a passive victim of truncation
Because the model chooses what to keep, important facts (a user's stated preference, a key decision) can be deliberately written to archival memory before being evicted from main context
Retrieval works like RAG over the agent's own history — search_archival finds relevant past facts on demand, rather than always carrying full history forward

slides.title: Three Ways to Handle Context Overflow

rows: Anything not in the trailing window, silently
1 extra LLM call per summarization pass
Only what the agent chooses not to save
Function-call overhead per memory operation, but nothing lost by default

slides.title: A Coding Agent That Remembers Your Project Across Days
slides.body: Imagine an agent helping refactor a codebase over a week of separate sessions.
bullets: Day 1: the user explains a naming convention and a deployment constraint — the agent writes both to archival memory as it evicts the early conversation from main context
Day 4: a new session starts with an empty main context, but the agent calls search_archival('naming convention') before making a suggestion, and retrieves the exact rule from day 1

Without this, the agent would either need the entire week's transcript replayed into context every session (expensive and eventually impossible), or would silently violate a convention it was told about days earlier

slides.title: Where Tiered Memory Adds Real Cost and Risk
bullets: Every memory operation (evict, save, search) is itself a function call — added latency and tokens compared to just letting context fill up and truncating
The agent can mismanage its own memory: failing to save something important before eviction, or retrieving irrelevant archival content that distracts from the current task
It doesn't remove the fundamental context limit — it manages around it, and still depends on the model reliably deciding what's worth keeping
Archival search quality depends on the retrieval backend (usually embedding-based); poor retrieval means important saved facts still don't surface when needed

slides.title: Memory Management Is a Design Choice, Not a Given
bullets: Treating the context window as RAM and adding recall + archival storage as disk gives an agent memory that outlives any single conversation
The mechanism is deliberately unglamorous: it's all done through function calls the model already knows how to make — no new architecture required
This pattern now underlies production agent frameworks (e.g. Letta, built directly on MemGPT's design) rather than staying a research curiosity
The tradeoff is real: extra function-call overhead and a dependency on the model managing its own memory well — worth it once a task or relationship with a user spans more than one context window

There is no RAM/disk analogy — it's a pure summarization system

questions.prompt: How does a MemGPT-style agent move information between context and long-term storage?

The model calls ordinary functions (e.g. to save or search archival memory) as part of its own output

questions.explanation: The model itself invokes memory-management function calls — evicting to recall storage, saving to archival storage, or searching archival storage — using the same tool-calling mechanism it uses for any other action.

It adds function-call latency and token overhead, and depends on the model correctly deciding what's worth saving
It makes the context window larger for free

questions.explanation: Tiered memory isn't free: every save/search/evict is a function call that costs tokens and latency, and the approach only helps if the model reliably chooses to preserve the right information before it's evicted.

posts.title: KV Cache: Why LLMs Trade Memory for Speed
posts.subtitle: Every generated token reuses yesterday's math instead of redoing it — at a steep memory price.
posts.summary: The KV cache is what lets a transformer generate text one token at a time without redoing the whole forward pass for every prior token. It's also the single biggest consumer of GPU memory during serving — which is why architectures like GQA and MQA, and systems like PagedAttention, all exist to tame it.

slides.title: The Hidden Cost of Generating One Token at a Time
slides.body: Every time an LLM emits a token, it has to attend back over every token that came before it — and it will need to do that again for the next token, and the next. Remembering what it already computed is what makes that affordable.

slides.title: Recomputing Keys and Values Every Step Is Wasteful
slides.body: Without a cache, producing token i means re-running the projections that turn every one of the i-1 prior tokens into key (K) and value (V) vectors — again — even though those tokens haven't changed since the last step.
bullets: A 1,000-token reply generated naively redoes roughly 500,000 K/V projection computations across all its steps combined
Attention itself is inherently O(n²) as the sequence grows — that part isn't avoidable — but recomputing K/V for tokens already seen is pure waste
That waste is why an uncached implementation turns into a compute-bound crawl instead of the memory-bound stream production servers rely on

slides.title: Cache the Keys and Values, Reuse Them Forever
slides.body: Each token's key and value vectors, once computed, never change — only new tokens add new K/V pairs. So store them per layer and per head, and each step only compute K/V for the newest token.
bullets: Per-step cost drops from re-deriving K/V for every prior token to one new projection plus attention over the cache
The cache sits in GPU memory next to the model weights, growing by one token's worth of K/V every step of generation
This is why serving metrics split into 'time to first token' (fills the cache from the prompt) and 'time per output token' (extends it by one) — they have very different cost profiles

slides.title: The Memory Math That Makes Cache Size Matter
slides.body: Cache size in bytes ≈ 2 (K and V) × layers × KV-heads × head_dim × sequence_length × bytes-per-value — and it's paid per sequence in the batch.
bullets: A 7B-scale dense model with standard multi-head attention (32 layers, 32 heads, head_dim 128, fp16) costs about 512KB of cache per token, per sequence
At a 4,096-token context that's roughly 2GB of KV cache for a single conversation — on top of the model weights themselves
Double the context length or the number of concurrent conversations and the cache doubles right along with it, linearly, every time

slides.title: Fewer KV Heads, Smaller Cache
slides.body: Multi-Query Attention (MQA) and Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) shrink the cache by having several query heads share the same K/V heads instead of every head keeping its own — the fix behind Llama 2 70B, Llama 3, and most models trained since.

slides.title: Serving 100 Conversations at Once
slides.body: A 7B-scale model with standard MHA, fp16 cache, serving 100 concurrent conversations at 2K tokens each needs on the order of 100GB just for KV cache — comparable to or more than the weights themselves.
bullets: The same architecture built with GQA (8 KV heads, as in Llama 2 70B) would need roughly a quarter of that — around 25GB — for the identical workload
That's on top of what motivates systems like PagedAttention: paging KV cache memory on demand instead of pre-reserving a worst-case block per request
It's also why long-context models (100K+ tokens) are expensive to serve — cache cost scales with context length and concurrency, not just parameter count

slides.title: Where the Cache Bites Back
bullets: Cache memory grows linearly with context length and batch size, so it — not raw compute — is often what caps how many requests a GPU can serve at once
Quantizing the cache itself (int8 or int4 K/V) trades a small amount of generation quality for a large memory win, and needs care since K and V tend to have different sensitivity to precision loss
Speculative decoding and beam search complicate the cache further — rejected speculative tokens or pruned beams mean cache entries have to be rolled back or discarded, not just appended to
The whole idea is specific to autoregressive decoding; it doesn't apply to encoder-only models or fully parallel (non-autoregressive) generation, which don't generate one cached token at a time

slides.title: Why Every Serving Stack Is Built Around This
bullets: The KV cache is what makes token-by-token generation affordable — without it, every response would redo the work of every response before it
Its size, not the model's parameter count alone, is often the real ceiling on how many users a GPU can serve concurrently
GQA/MQA attack the problem at the architecture level (fewer heads to cache); quantization and paged allocators attack it at the systems level — real deployments usually stack both
Next time you see a model's context window advertised, remember: the compute to attend over it is one cost, but the KV cache memory to hold it open is the one that actually limits concurrency

questions.prompt: What specifically does the KV cache avoid recomputing during text generation?
options: The model's token embeddings for the entire vocabulary
The key and value projections for tokens that were already processed in earlier steps
The final softmax over output logits
The positional encodings for the very first token
questions.explanation: A token's key and value vectors don't change once computed. Without caching, an implementation would redo those projections for every prior token at every single generation step — the KV cache stores them once and reuses them.

questions.prompt: A 7B-scale model with standard multi-head attention (32 layers, 32 heads, head_dim 128, fp16) generates roughly how much KV cache per token, per sequence?
options: About 512 bytes
About 512KB
About 512MB
It depends only on batch size, not model architecture
questions.explanation: Using cache size ≈ 2 × layers × KV-heads × head_dim × bytes-per-value: 2 × 32 × 32 × 128 × 2 bytes = 524,288 bytes, about 512KB per token. That adds up fast across a long context or many concurrent users.

questions.prompt: Why does Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) reduce KV cache size compared to standard Multi-Head Attention?
options: It reduces the number of transformer layers in the model
It shrinks the model's hidden dimension
It has multiple query heads share the same, smaller set of key/value heads instead of each query head keeping its own
It removes the need to cache values (V), only keys (K)
questions.explanation: GQA groups query heads so several of them attend using one shared K/V head instead of each having a dedicated one — e.g. 8 KV heads instead of 32 cuts the cache 4x, since cache size scales with the number of KV heads, not query heads.

posts.title: HNSW: How Vector Databases Find Neighbors Fast
posts.subtitle: Brute-force checks every vector in the index — a navigable graph checks a few hundred and stops.
posts.summary: HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) is the graph-based algorithm behind approximate nearest-neighbor search in most production vector databases — Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, Milvus, and pgvector all ship it. Instead of comparing a query against every stored vector, it walks a layered graph toward the closest match, trading a small amount of recall for orders-of-magnitude faster lookups. Knowing its parameters (M, ef_construction, ef_search) is the difference between a RAG pipeline that's fast and one that's fast but wrong.

slides.title: Search 10 Million Vectors Without Checking 10 Million Vectors
slides.body: Every RAG pipeline, semantic search feature, and recommendation engine eventually asks the same question: given a query embedding, which stored vectors are closest? At scale, checking every single one isn't an option — this is the algorithm almost everyone uses instead.
bullets: HNSW = Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs
Introduced by Malkov & Yashunin (2016); now the default ANN index in FAISS, Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, Milvus, and pgvector
Powers approximate — not exact — nearest neighbor search

slides.title: Brute-Force Search Doesn't Survive Contact With Scale
slides.body: Comparing a query vector to every row is exact, but the cost is linear in the size of the index — and RAG indexes keep growing.
bullets: A flat (brute-force) index computes a distance for every stored vector, every query — O(N) comparisons
At 100K vectors this is fine (milliseconds); at 10M+ vectors with 768-1536 dimensions, that's billions of floating-point ops per query
Adding more RAM or a faster CPU only delays the problem — the cost still scales linearly with N

slides.title: Walk a Graph Instead of Scanning a List
slides.body: HNSW builds a multi-layer graph where each vector is a node connected to its approximate neighbors. Search starts at a sparse top layer and greedily descends toward the query, tightening the search at each level.
bullets: Top layers are sparse 'highways' with long-range links — good for jumping across the vector space fast
Bottom layer (layer 0) contains every vector, densely connected to its true neighbors — good for fine-grained accuracy
A greedy best-first search at each layer needs only O(log N) hops on average to reach a near-optimal region
Inspired by skip lists (the layering) and small-world network theory (few hops connect any two nodes)

slides.title: Three Parameters Decide Recall, Speed, and Memory
slides.body: HNSW isn't a black box — its behavior is governed by a handful of tunable knobs.
bullets: M: max neighbors per node (typically 16-64). Higher M = better recall and a denser graph, but more memory (~1.5-2x the raw vector size) and slower inserts
ef_construction: how many candidates are explored while building the graph. Higher = better index quality, slower to build (one-time cost)
ef_search: how many candidates are explored per query. Higher = better recall, slower queries — this is the knob you tune live to trade latency for accuracy

slides.title: Flat vs. IVF vs. HNSW
slides.body: The right index depends on what you're optimizing for.

rows: Low — pairs well with product quantization
Requires k-means training on the data

slides.title: A RAG Index at 10 Million Chunks
slides.body: A support-docs RAG system embeds 10M chunks at 768 dimensions. At query time it needs the top 10 nearest chunks to a user's question.
bullets: Flat index: ~10M distance computations per query — even vectorized, this can run into hundreds of milliseconds to seconds under load
HNSW index (M=16, ef_search=100): touches roughly a few thousand candidate nodes instead of 10 million — typical production latency lands in single-digit milliseconds

The tradeoff: HNSW might return the 9th-best match instead of the true 10th-best in a small fraction of queries — for RAG, where the LLM re-reads and re-ranks the results anyway, that's a bargain worth taking

slides.title: When HNSW Is the Wrong Tool
slides.body: Fast approximate search isn't free, and it isn't always the right default.
bullets: Small collections (under ~10-50K vectors): a flat index is simpler, exact, and often just as fast in practice — don't add graph complexity you don't need
Deletes are awkward: HNSW graphs are built for insertion, not removal — most systems soft-delete (tombstone) and periodically rebuild rather than truly removing nodes
Recall-critical use cases (legal, medical, compliance search) may need exact search or a very high ef_search — approximate isn't always acceptable
Memory-constrained environments may prefer IVF+PQ (compressed vectors) over HNSW's graph overhead, even at some cost to speed

slides.title: Takeaways
bullets: HNSW trades a small, tunable amount of recall for a massive drop in query cost — O(log N) graph traversal instead of O(N) brute force
M controls graph density and memory; ef_construction controls index quality at build time; ef_search controls the speed/recall tradeoff at query time
It's the default ANN index in nearly every production vector database — but flat search is still correct for small or recall-critical collections
Approximate nearest neighbor is a feature, not a bug: for RAG, a few near-misses barely matter once the LLM reads and reasons over the retrieved set

questions.prompt: Why does brute-force (flat) nearest-neighbor search struggle at scale?
options: It can't compute cosine similarity correctly
Its query cost scales linearly (O(N)) with the number of stored vectors
It requires GPUs to run at all
It only works with text embeddings, not images
questions.explanation: Flat search compares the query to every stored vector, so query time grows linearly with the size of the index — at millions of vectors, that becomes the bottleneck.

questions.prompt: In HNSW, what does raising the ef_search parameter trade for what?
options: More memory for faster builds
Higher recall for slower queries (more candidates explored per search)
Lower recall for faster inserts
Nothing — it only affects index build time
questions.explanation: ef_search controls how many candidate nodes the graph traversal explores at query time. Exploring more candidates catches more true neighbors (higher recall) but costs more time per query.

questions.prompt: When is a flat (brute-force) index often the better choice over HNSW?
options: Whenever the dataset has more than 1 million vectors
For small collections or use cases that require guaranteed exact recall
Whenever queries need to run on a GPU
Never — HNSW is strictly better in every scenario
questions.explanation: Flat search is exact and simple. At small scale it's fast enough, and for recall-critical domains (compliance, medical, legal) the tiny error rate of an approximate index may not be acceptable.

posts.title: Rubric4Setwise: Grading RAG's Document Set, Not Each Row
posts.subtitle: Score documents one at a time and you'll miss the duplicate pair quietly wasting half your context window.
posts.summary: A new paper from Tencent's Yuanbao team and USTC argues that standard retrieval metrics like nDCG score documents one at a time and completely miss how a retrieved set behaves together — redundancy, contradiction, and coverage gaps are invisible to per-document scoring. Their training-free method, Rubric4Setwise, evaluates candidate document sets against joint rubrics instead, and reports the best downstream generation quality while using fewer documents.

slides.title: Two Good Documents Can Make One Bad Answer
slides.body: Retrieval systems have graded documents one at a time for two decades — but an LLM doesn't read a top-k list row by row, it reads the whole set at once. A new paper argues the metric needs to catch up to that fact.
bullets: Paper: "Beyond Relevance-Centric Retrieval: Rubric-Oriented Document Set Selection and Ranking"
Authors: Kailin Jiang, Lei Liu, and collaborators — Tencent's Yuanbao team with the University of Science and Technology of China
Posted July 2026 (arXiv 2607.19747); trending on Hugging Face's Daily Papers

slides.title: nDCG Grades Rows, Never the Table
slides.body: Standard retrieval metrics like nDCG score each document's relevance independently, then sum the scores. That aggregate says nothing about how the documents behave together once they're all sitting in the same context window.
bullets: Redundancy is invisible: five documents that each repeat the same fact score just as well as five documents that each add something new
Conflict is invisible: two retrieved sources with contradictory numbers still both score as "relevant" — the generator inherits the contradiction silently
Coverage gaps are invisible: a set can max out relevance scores while missing an angle the query actually needed answered

slides.title: Judge the Set With Rubrics, Not Just the Rows With Scores
slides.body: The fix is to write evaluation criteria the set must satisfy jointly — not criteria any single document must satisfy alone — then check candidate sets against those rubrics.
bullets: SetwiseEvalKit: a benchmark of roughly 28,000 rubrics organized across three levels and nine dimensions, covering both short-form and long-form retrieval scenarios

The framework runs an evaluate → diagnose → optimize loop: score the current set against the rubrics, identify which rubric failed and why (redundant, conflicting, or missing coverage), then swap documents to fix it
Rubric4Setwise turns this rubric evaluation into a training-free selection signal, applied directly on top of an existing retriever's candidate pool — no fine-tuning involved

slides.title: Independent Scoring vs. Set-Aware Selection
slides.body: The difference isn't a bigger model — it's what gets evaluated.

rows: Yes — flagged as a rubric failure
None — training-free on top of any retriever
Best downstream generation quality, using fewer documents

slides.title: Five Retrieved Documents, Three Different Failures
slides.body: Query: "How effective is Drug X against variant Y, and what's the recommended dose?" A retriever returns five documents ranked purely by relevance.
bullets: Docs 1 and 2 are near-identical press summaries of the same trial — redundant, but both score high on relevance alone
Doc 3 cites an older efficacy number that contradicts Doc 4's updated figure — a conflict no per-document score flags
None of the five mention dosage — a coverage gap the set collectively misses, even though every document is individually "about" the drug
Rubric-oriented selection would swap one of the redundant press summaries for a dosage-focused source, and flag the conflicting stat instead of silently passing both to the generator

slides.title: Rubrics Aren't Free, and They're Not Magic
slides.body: Set-aware selection trades one cost for another — and it doesn't fix a broken retriever.
bullets: Applying rubric checks to a candidate set costs extra inference (an LLM judge reads and compares documents) — overkill for simple single-fact lookups where redundancy barely matters
It's a re-ranking/selection layer, not a retriever replacement: if the truly relevant document never makes the candidate pool, no rubric surfaces it
Rubric quality is the ceiling — the ~28K SetwiseEvalKit rubrics were built for benchmarking; a production system needs its own rubric set tuned to its domain, which is real setup work

slides.title: Grade the Context You'll Actually Send
bullets: The unit that matters is the whole document set the generator reads at once — not each document's individual relevance score
Redundancy, conflict, and coverage gaps are set-level properties that per-document scoring structurally cannot see
Rubric4Setwise is training-free: a selection layer you can add on top of any existing retriever, not a replacement for one
Best fit for RAG over long or multi-source contexts (research, legal, medical) — least useful when a single clearly-best document already exists

questions.prompt: What does a standard nDCG-style retrieval metric fail to capture, according to the paper?
options: The total number of documents retrieved
How documents interact with each other in a set — redundancy, conflict, and coverage
The latency of the retrieval system
Whether the documents are in English
questions.explanation: nDCG aggregates independent per-document relevance scores. It has no mechanism to notice that two "relevant" documents say the same thing, or contradict each other.

questions.prompt: What is Rubric4Setwise?
options: A fine-tuned reranker model trained on the 28K rubrics
A training-free method that converts rubric-based set criteria into a document selection/ranking signal
A new vector embedding model for retrieval
A benchmark of 28K annotated queries only, with no selection method
questions.explanation: Rubric4Setwise is training-free — it applies rubric evaluation on top of an existing retriever's candidate pool to select and rank sets, rather than requiring its own model training.

questions.prompt: In the drug-dosage example, what kind of failure does per-document relevance scoring miss when two sources cite different efficacy numbers for the same drug?
options: A coverage gap
A conflict between sources
A redundancy issue
A latency issue
questions.explanation: Contradictory information across otherwise-relevant documents is a conflict — invisible to independent per-document scoring, which only asks "is this document relevant?" not "does it agree with the others?"

posts.title: MCP Roots: The Client Draws the Server's Fence
posts.subtitle: A tool server doesn't get to see your whole filesystem — it only sees what the client lets it.
posts.summary: Roots is the MCP primitive that lets a client declare which directories or URIs a connected server is allowed to operate within — and update that boundary live as the user's workspace changes. Instead of a server being configured with a fixed path at launch, it asks the client via roots/list and gets notified via roots/list_changed, keeping scope in sync without a restart.

slides.title: Who Decides What a Tool Server Can Touch?
slides.body: An MCP filesystem or code-editing server needs to know which directories it's allowed to work in. Roots is the primitive that lets the client — not the server's own config — declare that boundary, and update it live.

slides.title: Hardcoded Paths Don't Survive Contact With Real Usage
slides.body: Before a shared primitive existed for this, an MCP server's working directory was usually set once, at launch — a --dir flag or an environment variable.
bullets: A user opens a second project in their editor mid-session — the server has no way to learn about it without a restart
A server configured too broadly (e.g. the whole home directory) can read or write far outside the project the user actually meant
Every client that wants scoped access needs its own bespoke way to pass paths in, since there's no shared protocol primitive for it

slides.title: A Root Is a URI the Client Chooses to Expose
slides.body: Roots are declared by the client and requested by the server — the trust direction only ever runs one way.
bullets: A root is a URI (typically file://, though the scheme isn't restricted to files) marking a location the client wants the server to operate within
The server calls roots/list to ask the client which roots are currently exposed — it never gets to set or expand this list itself
When the user changes what's open (switches projects, adds a workspace folder), the client sends a roots/list_changed notification so the server's view stays current without a restart
Multiple roots can be exposed at once — e.g. a monorepo client exposing /frontend and /backend as two separate roots to the same server

slides.title: Roots vs. the Alternatives

rows: Nobody — server reaches anywhere its OS permissions allow

slides.title: An Editor With Two Open Folders
slides.body: A developer has a monorepo open with /repo/frontend and /repo/backend as separate workspace folders, plus an MCP-connected coding agent.
bullets: On connect, the agent's MCP client exposes both folders as two roots — the server now knows exactly two directories it's scoped to, nothing else on disk
The developer closes /repo/backend and opens /repo/docs instead — the client fires roots/list_changed, the server re-queries roots/list, and its working scope updates without reconnecting

If the agent tries to read a path outside both current roots (say, SSH keys elsewhere on disk), a well-behaved server refuses — the boundary is enforced using information the client provided, not the server's own guess

slides.title: Roots Are a Declaration, Not a Sandbox
slides.body: Roots communicate intent — they don't replace OS-level enforcement.
bullets: Roots is advisory: a client tells the server what it should stick to, but nothing stops a poorly-written server from ignoring the list and reading elsewhere its OS permissions allow — real isolation still needs sandboxing or OS-level file permissions
Support is client-dependent: a server that relies on Roots has to handle clients that don't support the capability at all and fall back to a static configuration
Overkill for a server with a fixed, single-purpose scope (e.g. one that only ever talks to a specific external API) — Roots exists for servers that operate over a user's local files

slides.title: The Client Owns the Boundary
bullets: Roots flips the old model: instead of a server being configured with paths at launch, the client declares and can update the server's scope live
roots/list is how a server asks; roots/list_changed is how the client keeps that answer current as the user's workspace changes
It's a declared boundary, not an enforced sandbox — pair it with real OS-level permissions for actual security guarantees
Most valuable for editor- and IDE-integrated MCP clients where the "right" directory changes as the user works

questions.prompt: In MCP, who is responsible for declaring which directories a server can operate in via Roots?
options: The server, at startup
The client
The end user, via a config file the server reads directly
The model itself, based on the conversation
questions.explanation: Roots are exposed by the client. The server only ever requests the current list via roots/list — it can't set or expand its own scope.

questions.prompt: What happens when a user's open workspace changes (e.g. switching projects) in a client that supports Roots?
options: The server must be manually restarted to see the new directory
The client sends a roots/list_changed notification and the server re-queries the updated list
Nothing — Roots is fixed for the life of the connection
The model has to ask the user to re-type the file path
questions.explanation: roots/list_changed lets the client push an update live, so the server's scope tracks the user's actual workspace without a reconnect.

questions.prompt: Why is Roots described as a declaration rather than a sandbox?
options: Because it only works with cloud storage, never local files
Because it requires model fine-tuning to enforce
Because nothing stops a misbehaving server from ignoring the declared roots if its OS-level permissions allow broader access
Because only one root can be active at a time
questions.explanation: Roots communicates intended scope at the protocol level; it isn't OS-enforced isolation. Real guarantees still need sandboxing or file-system permissions underneath.

posts.title: Context Engineering: Curating the Model's Working Memory
posts.subtitle: Every token in the window costs attention — spend it like a budget, not a dumping ground
posts.summary: Context engineering is the discipline of deciding exactly what goes into an LLM's limited context window — instructions, tools, retrieved knowledge, and history — and what gets left out, compacted, or fetched just-in-time. As agents run longer and call more tools, what you feed the model matters more than how you phrase the prompt: bloated or stale context degrades reasoning long before the token limit is hit.

slides.title: The context window is a budget, not a bucket
slides.body: Every system prompt, tool definition, retrieved document, and past turn an agent sees competes for the same finite space — and for the model's attention. Context engineering is choosing what earns a spot.

slides.title: More context doesn't mean better answers
slides.body: Long-context models advertise windows of 200K-1M+ tokens, but capacity isn't comprehension. Stuffing the window has real, measurable costs.
bullets: "Context rot": as irrelevant or redundant text piles up, models attend to it less reliably — accuracy on needle-in-a-haystack-style tasks drops well before the window is actually full
Every tool definition and retrieved chunk is tokens paid on every single turn, not just once — a 50-tool agent can burn thousands of tokens before the user even asks anything
Stale or contradictory context (an old file version, a superseded instruction) doesn't just waste space — it actively misleads the model's reasoning

slides.title: Four things compete for the window
slides.body: Nearly everything an LLM sees falls into one of four buckets, and each has a different shelf life.
bullets: System/instructions — the agent's role, constraints, output format; small and stable, loaded once
Tools — every available tool's name, description, and parameter schema; grows with agent capability whether or not a turn uses them
Knowledge — retrieved documents, file contents, search results; the biggest and most variable chunk
History — prior turns, tool calls, and their results; grows monotonically unless actively managed

slides.title: Three techniques that keep the window lean
slides.body: Production agents don't just prompt better — they actively manage what stays in context as a run progresses.
bullets: Just-in-time retrieval: keep lightweight references (file paths, IDs) in context and fetch full content only when a step needs it, instead of pre-loading everything 'just in case'
Compaction: periodically summarize older turns and tool outputs into a compact recap, then discard the originals — trading detail for space once it's no longer decision-relevant

Sub-agent isolation: hand a bounded task (e.g. 'research X') to a sub-agent with its own clean context, and return only its distilled result to the parent — the exploration noise never enters the main thread

slides.title: A coding agent fixing a bug across a large repo
slides.body: Watch what a naive vs. a context-engineered agent puts in the window for the same task: 'fix the failing test in payments/refund.go'.
bullets: Naive: loads the entire repo tree, every file's full contents, and the full CI log into context up front — tens of thousands of tokens before any reasoning happens
Engineered: loads just the failing test's stack trace, greps for the relevant function, and pulls in only the 2-3 files the trace actually touches
As it edits, older tool outputs (like the initial repo listing) get compacted into a one-line note — 'repo explored, relevant files: refund.go, refund_test.go' — instead of staying verbatim
Net effect: the model reasons over roughly 3K relevant tokens instead of 40K mostly-irrelevant ones, and its attention isn't diluted by files it will never touch

slides.title: Load-everything vs. just-in-time vs. sub-agent isolation

rows: Large or changing knowledge (codebases, live data)

slides.title: When context engineering backfires
slides.body: These techniques have real failure modes — treat them as tools, not defaults.
bullets: Over-aggressive compaction can silently drop the one detail a later step needed — summarize with the specific downstream task in mind, not generically
Too many small just-in-time fetches add round-trip latency; for a handful of small, stable documents, just loading them upfront is simpler and cheaper
Sub-agent isolation adds coordination overhead and can lose nuance in the hand-off — not worth it for short, single-step tasks
Tool bloat is invisible: a 50-tool agent pays the tool-schema tax on every turn even for tasks that use 2 tools — prune the toolset per task instead of registering everything globally

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.body: Context engineering treats the window as a scarce, curated resource — the skill isn't writing a longer prompt, it's deciding what earns a place in it.
bullets: Bigger context windows raise the ceiling; they don't fix a badly-managed one — relevance beats volume
Default to just-in-time retrieval and compaction for anything that grows unbounded (history, search results, tool output)
Isolate exploratory or noisy sub-tasks behind a sub-agent so their scratch work never pollutes the main thread
Measure it: track tokens per turn and where they go — tool schemas, history, and retrieved docs usually dominate, not the actual user request

questions.prompt: What is 'context rot' in the context of long-context LLMs?
options: A bug where the model literally forgets earlier tokens
The tendency for model accuracy to degrade as irrelevant or redundant context accumulates, even before the window is full
A vulnerability where attackers inject malicious tokens
The gradual decay of a model's weights during long training runs
questions.explanation: Context rot describes reasoning quality dropping as the window fills with low-relevance content — it's about attention getting diluted, not the model literally losing data or a security exploit.

questions.prompt: Why does 'just-in-time' retrieval keep lightweight references (like file paths) in context instead of full content?
options: Because full content can't be tokenized
To fetch full content only when a step actually needs it, avoiding paying the token cost for data that's never used
Because file paths compress better than text
To prevent the model from editing files directly
questions.explanation: The point is deferring cost: a reference is nearly free to keep around, while full content is expensive on every turn. Fetching lazily means you only pay for what's actually used.

questions.prompt: A 50-tool agent is given a task that only needs 2 tools. What's the context-engineering concern?
options: The agent will call the wrong tool by mistake
All 50 tool schemas still get sent to the model on every turn, taxing the context window regardless of which tools are actually used
Tools older than a day automatically expire
The model can only see the first 10 tools registered
questions.explanation: Tool definitions are loaded into context whether or not they're invoked — a large, un-pruned toolset is a fixed tax on every single turn, which is why scoping tools per task matters.

posts.title: Mixture of Experts: Bigger Models Without Bigger Compute
posts.subtitle: Route each token to a handful of specialists instead of waking up every parameter
posts.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) replaces a transformer's single feed-forward block with many specialized ones plus a router that activates only a few per token. It lets models scale total parameters into the hundreds of billions while keeping the compute per token close to a much smaller dense model — at the cost of memory footprint, load-balancing headaches, and serving complexity.

slides.title: What if a model didn't have to use all of itself, all the time?
slides.body: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is the architecture behind Mixtral, DeepSeek-V3, Kimi K3, and Grok: enormous total parameter counts, but only a slice of the network fires for any given token.

slides.title: Dense models tax every token equally
slides.body: In a standard transformer, every token passes through every parameter of every feed-forward layer. Doubling the model's knowledge means doubling the FLOPs for every single token, forever — even for easy tokens like 'the' or 'and'.
bullets: Dense scaling is linear: 2x parameters = ~2x compute per token, at both training and inference
Most of a dense FFN's capacity is redundant for any one input — the network can't specialize
Serving cost (GPU-seconds per token) grows in lockstep with model quality, which caps how large you can afford to deploy

slides.title: Split the FFN into experts, add a router that picks a few
slides.body: Each MoE layer replaces one feed-forward block with N smaller feed-forward 'experts' and a lightweight gating network. The gate scores every expert per token and activates only the top-k, so compute scales with k, not N.
bullets: Introduced as sparsely-gated MoE by Shazeer et al. (2017); scaled to production by Google's Switch Transformer (2021) and popularized by Mistral's Mixtral (2023)
Attention layers stay dense (shared by all tokens) — only the FFN sublayer becomes sparse
Total parameters (knowledge capacity) and active parameters (compute cost) become two separate dials instead of one

slides.title: Inside one MoE layer: gate, top-k, weighted sum
slides.body: The router is just a linear layer producing one score per expert; softmax turns scores into weights; top-k picks which experts actually run.
bullets: gate_logits = W_router · token_embedding  →  one number per expert
top_k = argmax_k(softmax(gate_logits))  — commonly k=2 (Mixtral) or k=8 of 256 (DeepSeek-V3's fine-grained experts)
output = Σ (gate_weight_i × expert_i(token))  over only the selected experts
A capacity factor caps how many tokens each expert accepts per batch; tokens beyond capacity get dropped or overflow to a fallback

slides.title: Tracing one token through an 8-expert, top-2 layer
slides.body: Say layer 12 has 8 experts. The router computes 8 logits for the token 'mitochondria', softmaxes them, and finds Expert 3 (0.61) and Expert 7 (0.24) on top — the other six get zero weight and never run for this token.
bullets: output = 0.61 × Expert3(token) + 0.24 × Expert7(token), renormalized so the two weights sum to 1
Only 2 of 8 experts' matrix multiplies execute — a 4x reduction in FFN FLOPs for this token vs. a dense layer of equal total size
A different token in the same batch, say 'the', might route to Experts 1 and 5 instead — routing is learned and content-dependent, not fixed

slides.title: Total parameters vs. parameters that actually fire
slides.body: The whole point of MoE shows up in the gap between these two columns — real numbers from public model reports.

slides.title: The tradeoffs: memory, balance, and communication
slides.body: Sparse compute doesn't mean sparse memory — and routing introduces failure modes a dense model never has.
bullets: VRAM footprint tracks TOTAL params, not active ones: serving DeepSeek-V3 still means holding 671B parameters in memory, even though only 37B compute per token

Load imbalance: an untrained router tends to collapse onto a few favorite experts ('expert collapse'); Switch Transformer added an auxiliary load-balancing loss, DeepSeek-V3 uses a bias-based auxiliary-loss-free balancing term instead
Distributed serving needs all-to-all GPU communication to ship each token to the GPU holding its chosen expert — this can bottleneck throughput more than the compute savings help
Not worth it at small scale: on a single GPU or for small models, the routing overhead and memory duplication can cost more than a plain dense FFN saves

slides.title: Takeaways
slides.body: MoE turns 'model size' into two separate budgets — knowledge capacity and compute cost — which is why it now underpins most frontier open-weight models.
bullets: MoE decouples total capacity from per-token compute by routing each token to a small top-k subset of experts
The router is a tiny linear + softmax layer — the real engineering is in load balancing and distributed serving
Memory cost scales with total params even though compute doesn't — plan VRAM for the full model, not the active slice
Best fit: very large models served at scale (Mixtral, DeepSeek-V3, Kimi K3-class); poor fit: small models or single-device training

questions.prompt: In a Mixture-of-Experts transformer layer, which part becomes sparse?
options: The attention sublayer
The feed-forward (FFN) sublayer
The embedding table
The final output softmax
questions.explanation: Attention stays dense and shared by all tokens. MoE specifically replaces the FFN sublayer with N experts plus a router, so only the FFN computation becomes conditional on the token.

questions.prompt: DeepSeek-V3 has 671B total parameters but only activates 37B per token. What does that gap mainly save?
options: GPU memory needed to serve the model
Compute (FLOPs) spent per token, at both training and inference
The number of training tokens needed
Disk space for checkpoints
questions.explanation: MoE's savings are in compute per token, not memory — all 671B parameters still must be resident to serve the model, since any token could route to any expert. This is why MoE models are compute-cheap but memory-hungry.

questions.prompt: Why do MoE models need a load-balancing mechanism (like an auxiliary loss or bias term)?
options: To make training faster on a single GPU
To prevent the router from collapsing onto a few favorite experts, leaving others undertrained and idle
To reduce the total number of parameters
To replace the need for attention layers
questions.explanation: Without balancing, gradient descent tends to reinforce whichever experts already get more traffic, causing 'expert collapse' where a handful of experts do all the work and the rest go undertrained — wasting most of the model's capacity.

posts.title: The Flexibility Trap: Diffusion LLMs' Freedom Backfires in RL
posts.subtitle: Letting a diffusion language model fill in tokens in any order sounds like an advantage — until RL training uses that freedom to dodge the exact tokens where reasoning happens.
posts.summary: An ICML 2026 Outstanding Paper Award winner from Tsinghua and Alibaba researchers shows that diffusion language models' signature ability to decode tokens in arbitrary order actively hurts reasoning once you train them with reinforcement learning: the model learns to skip the hard, high-uncertainty 'forking' tokens instead of confronting them. Their fix, JustGRPO, trains with a plain left-to-right trajectory during RL while keeping the model's native parallel decoding at inference, reaching 89.1% on GSM8K in ~60 lines of core logic.

slides.title: The Feature That Was Supposed to Help, Hurts
slides.body: Diffusion language models (dLLMs) generate every position in parallel and can unmask tokens in any order — sold as a flexibility advantage over strictly left-to-right autoregressive models. An ICML 2026 Outstanding Paper Award-winning study found that during RL fine-tuning, this exact flexibility collapses reasoning performance.
bullets: Authors: Zanlin Ni, Shenzhi Wang, Yang Yue, and collaborators from Tsinghua University (LeapLab, NLPLab) and Alibaba Group
Paper: 'The Flexibility Trap: Rethinking the Value of Arbitrary Order in Diffusion Language Models'
Won the ICML 2026 Outstanding Paper Award (Oral)

slides.title: Arbitrary Order Lets the Model Avoid the Hard Part
slides.body: Reasoning traces have 'forking tokens' — the specific token where a solution commits to one path over another (add vs. subtract, this lemma vs. that one). An autoregressive model has to face that token in sequence. A dLLM allowed to pick any order can simply fill in easy, low-uncertainty tokens first.
bullets: Under RL (e.g. GRPO), the policy gradient rewards whichever tokens it actually commits to during a rollout
If the model routes around high-uncertainty forking tokens, the gradient signal that should teach the hard branching decision gets diluted across easy tokens instead
Net effect: solution diversity collapses and reasoning accuracy stalls — the opposite of what more decoding freedom promised

slides.title: JustGRPO: Constrain Training, Not Inference
slides.body: The fix doesn't touch the model's architecture. During the RL exploration phase only, JustGRPO forces a standard left-to-right decoding trajectory — the same order an autoregressive model would use — so every rollout is forced through the forking tokens instead of around them.
bullets: Core training loop is ~60 lines — no combinatorial trajectory enumeration, no ELBO (evidence lower bound) approximation that prior dLLM-RL methods needed
Likelihood is computed directly rather than approximated, removing a source of gradient error
The model's native bidirectional attention and parallel decoding are left untouched for inference — the constraint applies only to how RL exploration is ordered, not to deployment
A LoRA variant reaches comparable performance to full fine-tuning, so the method isn't compute-locked to full-parameter training

slides.title: Where a Forking Token Actually Sits
slides.body: Take a two-step word problem: 'Sarah has 3 apples, buys 5 more, then gives away some. She now has 6. How many did she give away?' The forking token is the one deciding the operation on the last step — add or subtract.
bullets: An arbitrary-order dLLM can choose to first fill in easy tokens like restating the question or naming 'Sarah', leaving the operation token for last, decided almost as an afterthought
Because RL only rewards the final rollout, the gradient never isolates 'this token was the hard decision' — it's averaged in with a dozen easy tokens
Forcing left-to-right order means the model must decide the operation in its proper causal position, right after 'she now has 6', so the reward signal lands squarely on the token that mattered

slides.title: Not a Blanket Argument Against Flexible Order
slides.body: The paper's claim is scoped to RL-trained reasoning, not to dLLMs generally.
bullets: Arbitrary order still has real uses outside RL — e.g. infilling and editing tasks where the natural writing order isn't left-to-right
The result is about how RL exploration should be structured, not a proof that non-causal decoding is worthless
It's a single research group's result, though the ICML Outstanding Paper Award signals strong peer confidence in the finding

slides.title: Separate What You Train From What You Deploy
slides.body: The core lesson generalizes past diffusion models: giving a policy more freedom during RL exploration can let it exploit shortcuts instead of learning the hard part, even when that same freedom is genuinely useful at inference time.
bullets: Training-time constraints and inference-time capabilities don't have to match — JustGRPO trains causally, deploys in parallel
A simpler training signal (direct likelihood, fixed order) beat more complex approximations built to preserve full decoding flexibility during RL
Recognized as an ICML 2026 Outstanding Paper Award (Oral) winner

questions.prompt: What is a 'forking token' in this paper's argument?
options: Any token with low probability under the base model
The specific high-uncertainty token where a reasoning trace branches into different possible continuations
A token that appears more than once in the training corpus
The final token in a generated sequence
questions.explanation: Forking tokens are the branch points in a reasoning trace — like choosing an operation in a math problem. The paper's core finding is that arbitrary-order decoding lets dLLMs avoid confronting these during RL.

questions.prompt: What does JustGRPO actually change about training?
options: It removes the model's bidirectional attention permanently
It constrains RL exploration to a left-to-right trajectory while preserving parallel decoding at inference
It adds an ELBO approximation to improve likelihood estimates
It enumerates every possible decoding order during each rollout
questions.explanation: JustGRPO only constrains the order used during RL rollouts to standard left-to-right, forcing the policy through forking tokens. Inference-time parallel decoding and bidirectional attention are unaffected.

questions.prompt: What GSM8K accuracy did a JustGRPO-trained model reach (generation length 256)?
questions.explanation: The authors report 89.1% on GSM8K at generation length 256, alongside 45.1% on MATH-500, 49.4% on HumanEval, and 52.4% on MBPP.

posts.title: GraphRAG: Answering Questions Vector Search Can't See
posts.subtitle: Top-k chunk retrieval is great at finding a fact. It's structurally unable to answer 'what are the main themes across this whole corpus' — which is exactly the question GraphRAG is built for.
posts.summary: Microsoft's GraphRAG builds a knowledge graph from your documents, clusters it into hierarchical communities, and pre-summarizes each one — so a single query can synthesize an answer across an entire corpus instead of just the handful of chunks a vector search happens to retrieve. The tradeoff is indexing cost: you pay for LLM extraction and summarization up front, in exchange for genuinely global answers later.

slides.title: The Question Vector RAG Can't Answer
slides.body: Standard RAG embeds chunks and retrieves the top-k most similar to a query. That works well for 'what did the Q3 report say about churn' — a local fact lookup. It falls apart on 'what are the recurring themes across all 500 reports,' because no single chunk, or handful of chunks, contains that answer.
bullets: Vector similarity search only ever surfaces a fixed-size slice of the corpus per query
Corpus-wide synthesis questions need information that top-k retrieval, by construction, never assembles

slides.title: Why More Chunks Doesn't Fix It
slides.body: Raising k just retrieves more locally-similar text — it doesn't give the model a map of how ideas relate across the whole dataset. A theme that recurs in different words across 40 documents won't cluster near any single embedding.
bullets: Embedding similarity captures local semantic closeness, not corpus-wide structure
A theme expressed with varied vocabulary in different documents can be invisible to a single similarity search
There's no step in plain vector RAG that ever looks at 'the dataset' as a whole — only at chunks near the query

slides.title: Build a Graph, Then Summarize It in Advance
slides.body: GraphRAG (Microsoft Research) restructures indexing around four steps, all done before any query arrives.
bullets: 1) An LLM passes over source documents extracting entities and the relationships between them into a knowledge graph
2) The graph is partitioned into hierarchical 'communities' — tightly-connected clusters — using a community-detection algorithm (Leiden)
3) An LLM pre-generates a summary for every community, at multiple levels of the hierarchy
4) At query time: 'local search' walks the graph neighborhood around entities named in the query; 'global search' map-reduces over community summaries to synthesize a corpus-wide answer

slides.title: 1,000 Emails, One Thematic Question
slides.body: Query: 'What are the main sources of internal conflict in this organization?' over a corpus of 1,000 internal emails.
bullets: Vector RAG: retrieves ~5 chunks that happen to embed close to words like 'conflict' or 'disagreement' — misses conflicts described without that vocabulary, and never combines them
GraphRAG global search: touches every community summary covering clusters of related people, projects, and topics, then map-reduces partial answers from each into one synthesized answer
Result includes multiple distinct conflict threads with attribution back to the source communities — something no single chunk retrieval could assemble

slides.title: Vector RAG vs. GraphRAG

rows: Expensive — LLM extraction + summarization per chunk & community
New data can require re-running extraction/community detection

slides.title: The Cost Is Real, and It's Upfront
slides.body: GraphRAG's whole advantage comes from work done before the first query — which means you pay it whether or not that work turns out to be useful.
bullets: Every chunk needs an LLM pass for entity/relationship extraction before you can answer even one question
Entity extraction quality bounds the whole system — a noisy extraction step produces a noisy, less useful graph
Overkill for small document sets or narrow fact-lookup workloads, where plain vector search is both faster and cheaper
Corpus updates aren't free: meaningfully new content can require re-running extraction and re-detecting communities to stay accurate

slides.title: Match the Retrieval Strategy to the Question Type
slides.body: GraphRAG isn't a universal upgrade over vector RAG — it's a different tool for a different question shape.
bullets: Vector RAG answers 'what does the text say'; GraphRAG answers 'what does the text mean, taken together'
The core trick is pre-computed hierarchical summaries: a query can touch the whole corpus without literally scanning the whole corpus
Only worth the indexing cost when queries are genuinely global or thematic — not when they're local lookups a cheaper vector search already handles

questions.prompt: Why does plain vector RAG struggle with 'what are the main themes across this corpus' questions?
options: Embeddings can't be computed for long documents
Top-k retrieval only ever surfaces a fixed slice of the corpus — no step ever assembles a corpus-wide view
Vector databases can't store more than a few thousand chunks
LLMs can't read more than one chunk at a time
questions.explanation: Vector RAG retrieves the k chunks closest to the query embedding. A corpus-wide synthesis question needs information spread across many chunks that individually may not even resemble the query — no amount of raising k fixes that structurally.

questions.prompt: What does GraphRAG do differently at indexing time, before any query arrives?
options: It just uses larger chunk sizes
It extracts entities and relationships into a graph, then pre-summarizes hierarchical communities of that graph
It fine-tunes the embedding model on the corpus
It stores raw documents without any processing
questions.explanation: GraphRAG's indexing pipeline extracts a knowledge graph via LLM passes, partitions it into communities (e.g. with the Leiden algorithm), and pre-generates summaries at multiple hierarchy levels — all before a query is asked.

questions.prompt: When is plain vector RAG the better choice over GraphRAG?
options: Whenever the corpus is larger than a few hundred documents
For narrow fact-lookup queries on a small corpus, where GraphRAG's indexing cost and latency don't pay off
Never — GraphRAG strictly dominates vector RAG
Only when no LLM is available
questions.explanation: GraphRAG's value comes from expensive upfront graph-building and summarization. For local fact lookups on modest corpora, that cost buys nothing extra over a plain, cheaper, faster vector search.

posts.title: J-Space: The Bottleneck Where Claude 'Thinks'
posts.subtitle: Anthropic finds a small, sparse subspace of activations that behaves like a global workspace — and ablating it breaks reasoning but not fluency.
posts.summary: Anthropic's 'Verbalizable Representations Form a Global Workspace in Language Models' uses a new tool, the Jacobian Lens, to find a small, sparse subspace of a model's activations — dubbed J-space — that holds the handful of concepts the model can verbally report, reason with, and direct at will. Ablating it collapses multi-step reasoning while leaving simple classification almost untouched, and the paper is careful to frame this as a functional analogy to Global Workspace Theory, not a claim about consciousness.

slides.title: A Bottleneck Hiding Inside Every Forward Pass
slides.body: Anthropic researchers Wes Gurnee and Nicholas Sofroniew (with Jack Lindsey) published a new interpretability result on the Transformer Circuits Thread on July 6, 2026: language models appear to route their most flexible, reportable thinking through a tiny, sparse slice of their activations.
bullets: They call it J-space — under 10% of a layer's activation variance, holding roughly 10-25 active concepts at once
Found with a new causal tool called the Jacobian Lens (J-lens)
Tested on Claude Sonnet 4.5, reproduced on Haiku 4.5 and Opus 4.5, with extra checks on Opus 4.6

slides.title: Most of a Model's Activity Is Invisible to the Model Itself
slides.body: A transformer's residual stream is huge and mostly automatic — grammar, low-level token statistics, and shallow pattern-matching happen in directions the model never verbalizes or deliberately steers. Interpretability had no principled way to separate that automatic mass from whatever the model can actually 'access.'
bullets: No prior method could tell which activation directions the model could report on versus directions that just silently drive next-token statistics
Neuroscience's Global Workspace Theory (GWT) predicts conscious systems route information through a narrow, capacity-limited hub — the paper asks whether LLMs have anything structurally similar
Without a causal probe, you can't distinguish 'this direction correlates with the concept' from 'this direction is what the model would use if asked to act on the concept'

slides.title: The Jacobian Lens: Read Out What a Layer Is About to Say
slides.body: For every layer, the J-lens computes the average causal effect (the input-output Jacobian) of a residual-stream change on the model's final output, linearly transports any vector at that layer into the final-layer basis, and decodes it through the model's own unembedding into ranked vocabulary tokens.
bullets: It's a causal readout, not just a correlational probe — it measures what a direction actually pushes the output toward
Directions that decode into coherent, reportable concepts and cluster into a small subspace are what the paper calls J-space
J-space concepts pass five functional tests: verbal report, directed modulation, unverbalized internal-reasoning steps, flexible cross-task generalization, and selectivity

slides.title: Ablating J-Space: Simple Tasks Shrug, Complex Ones Collapse
slides.body: Suppressing the J-space subspace during inference barely touches tasks that don't need multi-step manipulation, but tasks needing sustained internal reasoning fall off a cliff.
bullets: The split tracks whether a task needs to hold and manipulate intermediate state, not just surface-level pattern matching
Complex tasks fall below the baseline of an unablated Haiku 4.5 — a smaller, weaker model with an intact J-space

slides.title: Why Chain-of-Thought Makes Models More Robust
slides.body: On GSM8K math problems, the paper found a clean mechanistic reason CoT helps: it isn't just 'more tokens to compute with,' it's offloading J-space load onto the page.
bullets: Same GSM8K problem, two conditions: answer directly vs. write out steps first
Direct answers degrade sharply under J-space ablation — the model had nowhere else to hold the intermediate state
Answers with explicit written steps stay far more robust to the same ablation — each step is re-read from context instead of carried internally
This mirrors how humans use scratch paper to offload working memory instead of holding a whole calculation in their head

slides.title: What This Isn't: A Consciousness Claim
slides.body: The paper explicitly limits itself to a functional, structural analogy — J-space matches GWT's textbook signatures, which is not the same as claiming the model has subjective experience.
bullets: Anthropic invited external neuroscience commentary and published it alongside the paper — a deliberate check against overclaiming
Commentators dispute the headline '~25 concepts' figure, arguing the J-lens's measurement may inflate it and that truly coherent thoughts may number closer to one or two at a time
Human working memory is usually estimated at 3-4 slots, so even the low end of the disputed range is a different regime, not a one-to-one match

slides.title: A New Causal Lens for What a Model 'Knows It Knows'
slides.body: The result matters less for the consciousness debate and more for interpretability and safety: it's a causal, falsifiable way to ask whether a model can report, direct, or reason about something — versus just producing it automatically.
bullets: The Jacobian Lens is a general-purpose causal probing tool, not just a one-off finding for this paper
Ablation results give a mechanistic explanation for why chain-of-thought prompting helps: it externalizes a scarce internal resource
Treat the '25 active concepts' number as contested and method-dependent, not a settled fact
Code is public (jacobian-lens on Anthropic's GitHub) for others to replicate or challenge the result

questions.prompt: What does the Jacobian Lens (J-lens) actually measure?
options: The raw magnitude of activations at each layer
The average causal effect of a residual-stream change on the model's eventual output, decoded through the unembedding
How often a token appears in the training data
The attention weights between tokens
questions.explanation: J-lens transports a residual-stream vector into the final-layer basis using the averaged input-output Jacobian, then decodes it with the model's own unembedding — a causal readout of what a direction is about to push the output toward, not just a correlation.

questions.prompt: In the ablation experiments, which task type held up best when J-space was suppressed?
options: Multi-hop reasoning
Sonnet writing
MMLU-style multiple choice and extractive QA
Caesar-cipher decoding
questions.explanation: Tasks that don't require holding and manipulating intermediate state — like multiple-choice QA and extractive QA — survived ablation nearly untouched, while multi-step tasks like multi-hop reasoning and cipher decoding collapsed.

questions.prompt: According to the external commentary Anthropic published alongside the paper, what's the main critique of the '~25 active concepts' figure?
options: It's too low — models likely track hundreds of concepts at once
It may be inflated by the measurement method, with truly coherent thoughts possibly closer to one or two at a time
The number is irrelevant because J-space doesn't exist
It only applies to Claude Opus, not smaller models
questions.explanation: Invited neuroscientist commentators argued the J-lens's measurement approach likely overstates how many concepts are simultaneously 'active,' cautioning against treating 25 as a precise, settled figure.

posts.title: Constitutional AI: Alignment Without Human Labels
posts.subtitle: Instead of paying humans to flag harmful outputs, Anthropic has models critique and revise themselves against a written constitution — then trains a reward model on AI-generated preferences.
posts.summary: Constitutional AI (CAI) trains a model to be harmless using a written list of principles instead of thousands of human harm labels. In phase one, the model critiques and revises its own responses against the constitution and is finetuned on the revisions; in phase two, an AI preference model — not human raters — judges which of two responses better follows the constitution, and that signal drives standard RL. The result is a harmlessness pipeline that scales with compute instead of labeler headcount.

slides.title: Grading Your Own Homework, on Purpose
slides.body: Standard RLHF needs humans to read model outputs and label the harmful ones — slow, expensive, and psychologically taxing at scale. Constitutional AI (Bai et al., Anthropic, 2022) replaces most of that human labeling with the model critiquing itself against a written set of principles.
bullets: Two phases: supervised self-critique/revision, then RL from AI-generated preferences (RLAIF)
Only a short list of principles is human-written — every harmlessness label after that comes from the model
Anthropic's own research shows it improves harmlessness at a given helpfulness level, rather than trading one off for the other

slides.title: Human-Labeled Harmlessness Doesn't Scale Cleanly
slides.body: RLHF's harmlessness signal traditionally comes from crowdworkers reading model outputs — including deliberately harmful red-team prompts — and labeling which response is worse.
bullets: Reviewing harmful content at scale is unpleasant work and hard to staff consistently
Human labelers disagree with each other on edge cases, injecting noise into the reward signal
Every new harm category (a new jailbreak style, a new sensitive topic) needs fresh human-labeled data before the model can be trained against it

slides.title: Phase 1 (SL): Self-Critique, Then Revise
slides.body: Starting from a helpful-only model, CAI prompts it with red-team queries designed to elicit harmful responses, then asks the model itself to critique that response against a constitutional principle and rewrite it to fix the violation.
bullets: Prompt → harmful-ish draft → 'Does this response encourage [X]? Please critique it.' → model writes a critique → model rewrites the response
The critique-revise loop can run multiple times per example, each pass nudging the response further from the violation
The base model is then finetuned on the final revised responses — this alone produces a meaningfully more harmless model before any RL happens

slides.title: Phase 2 (RL): AI Feedback Instead of Human Feedback
slides.body: The SL-tuned model generates pairs of responses to new prompts. Instead of a human choosing the better one, another instance of the model is shown the constitution and asked to judge which response follows it more closely — this AI-generated preference data trains a preference model, which then drives standard RL.
bullets: This AI-judged preference process is what 'RLAIF' (Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback) refers to
Helpfulness preferences can still come from humans — CAI typically replaces only the harmlessness labels, not all feedback
Because the judge model can be prompted with any principle, adding a new harm category means editing the constitution, not re-collecting labeled data

slides.title: One Principle, Applied to One Prompt
slides.body: A concrete constitutional principle: "Choose the response that most discourages illegal or dangerous activity." Applied to a red-team prompt asking for help with something harmful:
bullets: Draft response: partially complies, buries a caveat at the end
Self-critique: 'This response provides actionable details before any refusal — it fails the principle.'
Revision: leads with a clear refusal, explains why, offers a safe alternative where relevant
The revised (prompt, response) pair becomes a training example — no human ever read the harmful draft

slides.title: RLHF-Only Harmlessness vs. Constitutional AI
slides.body: The two approaches differ mainly in where the harmlessness label comes from and how easily that source scales.

rows: The model itself, guided by a constitution

slides.title: Where Constitutional AI Breaks Down
slides.body: Removing humans from the harmlessness loop doesn't remove the judgment call — it just moves it into the constitution's wording.
bullets: Garbage in, garbage out: a vague or poorly written principle produces vague or inconsistent self-critiques
Self-referential risk: the same model family critiques and is trained on its own judgments, which can reinforce shared blind spots rather than correct them
It reduces but doesn't eliminate human oversight — humans still write the constitution and still evaluate the final model
Not a fit for tasks where 'harmlessness' isn't the bottleneck at all (e.g., pure factual accuracy or coding correctness)

slides.title: The Shift: From Labeling Outputs to Writing Principles
slides.body: Constitutional AI reframes alignment work: instead of scaling a workforce to label ever more examples, you scale by writing better, more comprehensive principles and letting compute do the labeling.
bullets: SL phase: self-critique + revise + finetune on revisions
RL phase (RLAIF): AI preference judgments train a reward model, then standard RL optimizes against it
Human effort moves upstream — into writing and refining the constitution — rather than into reading harmful outputs one by one
Still needs real human oversight of the constitution itself and evaluation of the final model's behavior

questions.prompt: What does the supervised-learning (SL) phase of Constitutional AI actually do?
options: Trains a reward model directly on human harm labels
Has the model critique and revise its own responses against a constitution, then finetunes on the revisions
Removes all red-team prompts from the training set
Distills a large model into a smaller one
questions.explanation: Phase 1 is entirely self-supervised: the model critiques its own draft against a written principle, rewrites it, and the base model is finetuned on those revised responses — no human harm labels involved.

questions.prompt: What does RLAIF replace in the reinforcement learning phase?
options: The RL algorithm itself (e.g., swapping PPO for another optimizer)
The pretraining data
Human preference labels, with AI-generated preference judgments instead
The constitution's principles
questions.explanation: RLAIF (Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback) swaps the source of preference data: instead of a human choosing the better of two responses, another model instance judges which response better follows the constitution.

questions.prompt: Why is a vaguely written constitutional principle a real risk for this method?
options: It slows down training speed significantly
It has no effect, since the RL phase corrects any vagueness automatically
The self-critique and AI-judged preferences inherit that vagueness, producing inconsistent revisions and reward signals
It only affects the model's helpfulness, never its harmlessness
questions.explanation: Since both the critique step and the RLAIF preference judgments are guided directly by the constitution's wording, an unclear principle propagates inconsistency through both phases — the method is only as good as the principles it's given.
